reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Choledocholithiasis is the presence of gallstones in the common bile duct, usually having migrated from the gallbladder, and may be silent or cause obstruction
Typical features are right upper quadrant or epigastric pain with obstructive jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine, and it is a leading cause of extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Liver function tests show a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern with raised bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-GT, and a duct dilated above the stone may be seen on ultrasound
It is an important cause of gallstone pancreatitis when a stone obstructs at the ampulla and of ascending cholangitis when the obstructed duct becomes infected
MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are accurate for confirming ductal stones when ultrasound is inconclusive but clinical suspicion is moderate to high
ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is both diagnostic and therapeutic, while stones can also be cleared surgically at cholecystectomy via the cystic duct or the common bile duct
Because the gallbladder remains the source of stones, cholecystectomy is generally advised after ductal clearance to prevent recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Common bile duct stones are usually cholesterol or mixed stones that form in the gallbladder and pass through the cystic duct into the common bile duct; primary duct stones (typically pigment stones) form within the duct, favoured by biliary stasis, stricture, or infection. A stone obstructing the duct raises biliary pressure and causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and cholestasis. Obstruction at the ampulla can block pancreatic outflow and trigger acute pancreatitis. Stagnant, obstructed bile readily becomes infected, and rising ductal pressure allows bacteria and endotoxin to translocate into the circulation, producing ascending cholangitis and potentially biliary sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Acute cholecystitis or biliary colic without ductal stones
Malignant biliary obstruction (pancreatic head or cholangiocarcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests demonstrating a cholestatic pattern
Transabdominal ultrasound for ductal dilatation and gallbladder stones
MRCP for non-invasive delineation of ductal stones
Endoscopic ultrasound in equivocal or intermediate-probability cases
ERCP as combined diagnostic and therapeutic intervention
Intraoperative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound at cholecystectomy
Blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and coagulation profile when cholangitis is suspected
redFlags: Ascending cholangitis with Charcot triad (fever with rigors, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), or Reynolds pentad with hypotension and confusion indicating biliary sepsis requiring urgent decompression
Septic shock or organ dysfunction from an obstructed, infected biliary tree
reference.prognosis: With timely stone clearance and, where appropriate, cholecystectomy the outlook is excellent and complications are prevented. Prognosis is worse when choledocholithiasis is complicated by severe cholangitis or pancreatitis, especially with delayed biliary decompression, but urgent drainage markedly improves survival in cholangitis.
pitfalls: Overlooking ductal stones in a patient with only mildly abnormal liver tests or a non-dilated duct on early ultrasound
Delaying biliary decompression in cholangitis while pursuing further imaging
Performing cholecystectomy without clearing the duct, leaving retained stones
Failing to recognise a stone impacted at the ampulla as the cause of gallstone pancreatitis
Attributing obstructive jaundice to stones and missing an underlying malignant stricture
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Clear the duct endoscopically with ERCP, biliary sphincterotomy and stone extraction as the mainstay of treatment
Perform cholecystectomy to remove the gallbladder source of stones, either after endoscopic clearance or with combined laparoscopic bile-duct exploration
Use mechanical lithotripsy or cholangioscopy-guided laser or electrohydraulic lithotripsy for large or impacted stones
Treat ascending cholangitis urgently with broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency biliary decompression and drainage
Manage associated gallstone pancreatitis with supportive care and early biliary decompression when obstruction persists
Monitor liver function to confirm resolution of the cholestatic pattern and adequate duct clearance
